CausalChain: Fasting -> Energy Stress in HCC Cells -> Upregulation/Restoration of miR-199a-5p and Other miRNAs (e.g., miR-202) -> Direct Downregulation of HK2 and PKM2 (via validated CRISPR screens and binding assays) -> Shift from Aerobic Glycolysis (Warburg Effect) -> Enhanced Oxidative Phosphorylation -> Lower Lactate Production -> Diminished Lactate-Mediated Immune Evasion -> Enhanced Sorafenib Sensitivity
Hypothesis: We propose that, in HCC, intermittent fasting generates an energy-limited microenvironment that not only counteracts the typical downregulation of miR-199a-5p seen in tumors but also stimulates a broader miRNA network including miR-202. This network directly targets and suppresses the glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2. As a direct consequence, the metabolic machinery shifts away from high-rate aerobic glycolysis to a state favoring oxidative phosphorylation. The reduction in lactate production blunts the immunosuppressive tumor microenvironment, thereby reactivating anti-tumor immune responses and enhancing the tumor’s sensitivity to sorafenib. To rigorously test this hypothesis, we will deploy advanced genomic editing (CRISPR-based screens), high-resolution single-cell metabolomics, and state-of-the-art imaging techniques, alongside immunophenotyping approaches, to ensure both mechanistic clarity and translational relevance.
Abstract: Recent evidence highlights the central role of miRNA-mediated metabolic reprogramming in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). We hypothesize that intermittent fasting induces a transient energy stress in HCC cells that restores and modulates a network of miRNAs—including miR-199a-5p, miR-202, and potentially others—to directly target critical glycolytic enzymes HK2 and PKM2. This coordinated downregulation shifts metabolism from a Warburg phenotype toward increased oxidative phosphorylation, leading to lowered lactate production. The resultant decrease in lactate alleviates lactate-mediated immune evasion, thereby restoring immune surveillance and enhancing the efficacy of sorafenib. Modern tools, including CRISPR-based transcriptomic screening, single-cell metabolomics, advanced live-cell imaging, and immunophenotyping, will be integrated to validate each step. This approach not only refines our understanding of fasting-induced metabolic shifts but also informs metabolically targeted immunotherapeutic interventions for liver cancer.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis posited that fasting-induced energy stress elevates miR-199a-5p, which downregulates HK2 and PKM2 leading to reduced glycolysis and enhanced sorafenib sensitivity. The revised hypothesis incorporates additional miRNAs (e.g., miR-202) to reflect the complexity of miRNA networks in HCC, acknowledges the observed downregulation of miR-199a-5p in tumors, and frames fasting as a means to counteract this deficit. Moreover, it expands the causal chain by clearly integrating modern technologies to validate each step, provides a more detailed mechanism for how metabolic reprogramming leads to immunomodulation via diminished lactate production, and refines the transition from metabolic alterations to improved sorafenib responsiveness. In each step—fasting inducing energy stress, miRNA upregulation, direct targeting of glycolytic enzymes, metabolic switching, reduced immunosuppression, and finally enhanced drug sensitivity—the revised hypothesis directly reflects and augments the original causal reasoning with contemporary experimental strategies.
